domainCoverage.synopsis: Concurrency race conditions are non-deterministic, hard to reproduce, and catastrophic under load. This volume deconstructs CPU memory models, lock-free atomics, distributed locking, Redlock consensus, and reactive streams.

chapters.title: Memory Models & Happens-Before
chapters.summary: A memory model defines the exact rules under which writes by one CPU core become visible to another, using a formal partial order called happens-before to constrain compiler reordering, CPU store buffers, and out-of-order execution.

chapters.title: Lock-Free Atomics
chapters.summary: Lock-free atomics coordinate shared state across threads using hardware compare-and-swap (CAS) primitives and explicit memory orderings so at least one thread always makes progress without OS mutex blocking.

chapters.title: Goroutine Worker Pools
chapters.summary: A goroutine worker pool bounds concurrency by running a fixed set of N lightweight goroutines pulling jobs from a shared channel, giving you predictable memory, backpressure, and clean cancellation via context.Context.

chapters.title: Python GIL-Free Concurrency, Asyncio & Coroutines
chapters.summary: Free-threaded Python (PEP 703, CPython 3.13t+) removes the Global Interpreter Lock so multiple threads execute Python bytecode simultaneously across CPU cores within a single shared memory space.

chapters.title: Pessimistic Locking Strategies
chapters.summary: A concurrency control approach that acquires exclusive or shared locks before reading or modifying data, serializing conflicting writers upfront to prevent lost updates.

chapters.title: Deadlock Detection & Prevention
chapters.summary: Identifying and resolving circular wait conditions—where two or more threads or database transactions hold locks each other needs—via wait-for graph cycle detection, timeouts, or canonical lock ordering.

chapters.title: Async/Await & Deadlock Avoidance
chapters.summary: Async/await turns non-blocking I/O into sequential-looking state machines, but mixing synchronous blocking calls, single-threaded event loops, or non-async-aware locks can freeze an entire runtime.

chapters.title: Thread Pool Design
chapters.summary: A thread pool bounds concurrency by reusing a fixed or elastic set of worker threads over a task queue, preventing OS thread exhaustion (~1 MB stack per thread) and CPU thrashing under burst traffic.

chapters.title: Reactive Streams Backpressure
chapters.summary: Reactive Streams backpressure is a non-blocking, pull-based flow-control protocol where downstream consumers explicitly signal how many items (`request(n)`) they can process, preventing fast producers from overwhelming slow consumers.

chapters.title: Actor Model Concurrency
chapters.summary: The Actor Model structures concurrent systems as isolated, share-nothing entities (actors) that encapsulate private state and communicate exclusively via asynchronous message passing into per-actor mailboxes (e.g., Erlang/OTP `GenServer`, Akka/Pekko, Microsoft Orleans).

chapters.title: ACID Transaction Fundamentals
chapters.summary: ACID guarantees that database transactions execute as all-or-nothing units (Atomicity), preserve schema and domain invariants (Consistency), shield concurrent readers/writers from partial state (Isolation), and survive power loss once acknowledged (Durability) via write-ahead logging (WAL), `fsync`, and concurrency control (MVCC/2PL).

chapters.title: Database Isolation Levels & Transaction Anomalies
chapters.summary: Database isolation levels control what concurrent transaction anomalies—dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads, and write skew—are permitted in exchange for lower locking or coordination overhead.

chapters.title: Optimistic Concurrency Control
chapters.summary: A lock-free concurrency pattern that lets readers and writers proceed without blocking, validating at commit time via a version number or ETag that no one else modified the record.

chapters.title: Distributed Locking & Redlock Algorithm
chapters.summary: Distributed locking coordinates mutually exclusive access to a shared resource across independent processes that share no memory, using a network-accessible lease store such as Redis, etcd, or ZooKeeper.

chapters.title: Split-Brain Prevention
chapters.summary: Split-brain happens when a network partition splits a distributed cluster into isolated groups that both elect a primary and accept conflicting writes; preventing it requires strict majority quorums (N/2 + 1), time-bounded leases, and monotonic fencing tokens.

domainDeepDive.whatIsThisDomain: Distributed concurrency and multithreading govern how independent execution threads and distributed cluster nodes coordinate access to shared state without data corruption, deadlocks, or priority inversion. It spans hardware memory models and atomic CPU instructions up to distributed lock consensus, fencing tokens, and reactive backpressure flow control.
domainDeepDive.whyItMatters: Concurrency race conditions are non-deterministic, notoriously difficult to reproduce in development environments, and catastrophic under production load. A subtle race condition can silently corrupt financial balances, allocate duplicate seats on flights, or deadlock database thread pools, freezing entire systems without emitting explicit error logs. Mastering memory barriers, compare-and-swap (CAS) primitives, and distributed fencing tokens is the hallmark of elite systems engineers.
domainDeepDive.keyTakeaway: At scale, any possible thread interleaving or network delay will occur. Never rely on shared mutable state without synchronization; minimize critical sections, enforce lock hierarchies, and use monotonically increasing fencing tokens across distributed boundaries.
coreArchitectureRules: Hardware Memory Model & Happens-Before Guarantee: Modern CPUs reorder instructions aggressively and cache values in L1/L2 registers. Memory barriers and volatile/atomic semantics must be used to guarantee that updates made by one thread are visibly published to others.

Compare-And-Swap (CAS) & Lock-Free Progress: Lock-free algorithms rely on hardware atomic primitives (CAS) to update state optimistically without thread suspension, eliminating lock acquisition contention and priority inversion.
The Distributed Lock Fencing Invariant: A distributed lock without a monotonically increasing fencing token cannot protect shared resources against client garbage collection pauses or network delays.

Linearizability vs Serializability: Linearizability guarantees that every operation appears to take effect instantaneously at a point in time between its invocation and response in real time. Serializability guarantees operations execute as if sequential, but without real-time ordering constraints.

Deadlock Prevention via Strict Lock Ordering: To prevent circular wait deadlocks across multiple resources (A and B), all execution threads must acquire locks in the exact same predefined global order.

failureModes.name: The Stale Lock Zombie Writer (GC Pause Disaster)
failureModes.description: Client 1 acquires a Redis distributed lock with a 30s TTL to write a file to S3. Client 1 experiences a 35s JVM Stop-The-World GC pause. The lock expires. Client 2 acquires the lock and writes file v2. Client 1 unpauses and writes stale file v1, corrupting storage.
failureModes.mitigation: Issue a monotonically increasing fencing token with each lock grant. The storage layer checks the fencing token and rejects any write with a token lower than the maximum token committed.

failureModes.name: Hidden Race Condition (Check-Then-Act Anti-Pattern)
failureModes.description: Two concurrent requests check if a user balance is >= $100. Both read $100 simultaneously, both approve the withdrawal, and both write $0, causing a double-spend overdraft.
failureModes.mitigation: Use atomic database transactions with optimistic locking (UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 100), or serialized Redis Lua scripts.

failureModes.name: Circular Wait Deadlock Across Microservices
failureModes.description: Transaction 1 locks record X and requests a lock on record Y. Concurrently, Transaction 2 locks record Y and requests a lock on record X. Both threads block indefinitely, consuming connections until the pool is exhausted.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce consistent global lock ordering, configure aggressive lock acquisition timeouts, and implement automated deadlock detection that aborts and retries the newer transaction.

failureModes.name: Unbounded Queue Memory Starvation
failureModes.description: A high-speed producer pushes events into an unbounded in-memory worker queue. Consumers process items slower than arrival rate. The queue grows silently until the JVM crashes with java.lang.OutOfMemoryError.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce bounded queues with explicit rejection policies (drop oldest, drop latest, or caller-runs), and implement reactive backpressure signals to slow down producers.

domainContent.title: Distributed Concurrency & Multithreading

spark.summary: Distributed concurrency and multithreading govern how execution threads and cluster nodes coordinate shared state without data corruption, deadlocks, or resource starvation. It spans CPU memory models and lock-free atomics up to distributed fencing tokens, thread-pool sizing, and reactive backpressure.
spark.keyTakeaway: At scale, every possible thread interleaving and network pause will happen. Minimize shared mutable state, establish strict happens-before edges, enforce global lock ordering, and validate distributed leases with monotonic fencing tokens.

domain.purpose: Concurrency bugs are non-deterministic, invisible under low local load, and catastrophic in production—silently corrupting balances, double-booking inventory, or freezing thread pools without throwing exceptions. Correct concurrent systems require reasoning from physical silicon (MESI cache coherence, memory barriers, CAS) through OS/runtime scheduling (futexes, M:N coroutines, bounded queues) up to distributed safety invariants (fencing tokens, linearizability, backpressure).
audience: Software engineers preparing for concurrency, multithreading, and distributed systems interviews.
Backend and systems engineers building high-throughput, low-latency services and storage engines.
Technical leads eliminating race conditions, deadlocks, and tail-latency stalls in production.
learningOutcomes: Establish formal happens-before visibility across CPU store buffers using Acquire-Release semantics and hardware memory barriers.
Choose between OS kernel threads, M:N user-space coroutines, and single-threaded event loops based on context-switch cost and blocking behavior.
Analyze mutex fast-path/slow-path futex mechanics, spinlock hazards, and read-write lock starvation.
Build or evaluate lock-free CAS loops while preventing the ABA problem via tagged pointers and safe memory reclamation.
Eliminate deadlocks, livelocks, and priority inversion using Coffman-condition breaking, Wait-For Graphs, and Little's Law thread-pool bounds.
Implement demand-driven reactive backpressure and monotonic distributed fencing tokens to survive slow consumers and GC pauses.

learningJourney.title: CPU Memory Models, Cache Coherence & Atomics
learningJourney.purpose: Understand how CPU store buffers, MESI cache coherence, and memory barriers govern cross-core visibility.
learningJourney.explanation: Multi-core CPUs achieve high IPC by buffering writes in per-core store buffers and speculatively reordering loads ahead of stores. Even x86 Total Store Order (TSO) allows a core to read stale values before its own store buffer drains, while weak memory models like ARM64 and POWER reorder both loads and stores aggressively. Cache coherence protocols (MESI/MOESI) ensure all cores eventually see a consistent single-address history via cache-line invalidation messages, but visibility ordering between different addresses requires explicit happens-before edges. Acquire-Release atomics prevent reads from hoisting before a lock acquire and writes from sinking past a lock release without paying full Sequential Consistency (`seq_cst`) fence costs.

ideas.title: Acquire-Release Happens-Before
ideas.description: A store-release in Thread A synchronizing with a load-acquire in Thread B guarantees all prior writes in A are visible to all subsequent reads in B.

ideas.title: MESI Invalidation & False Sharing
ideas.description: Writing to any byte of a 64-byte cache line invalidates that entire line in peer L1/L2 caches; pad independent atomic variables to 64-byte boundaries.

example.title: Fixing an intermittent ARM64 ring-buffer race
example.scenario: A C++ single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer passed all tests on x86_64 servers but intermittently read uninitialized payload slots after migrating to ARM64 Graviton instances.
example.reasoning: On x86 TSO, stores are ordered with respect to other stores, masking a missing fence; on ARM64's weak memory model, the consumer observed the updated `write_idx` before the payload write landed. Upgrading `write_idx` to `memory_order_release` and `memory_order_acquire` emitted lightweight `stlr`/`ldar` barriers and eliminated the race.
example.lesson: Never rely on x86 TSO accidents for cross-thread visibility; encode explicit acquire-release happens-before edges.

reflectionQuestions: Which shared variables lack an explicit happens-before edge (mutex, acquire-release atomic, or channel handoff)?
Have you tested lock-free or atomic code on weak-memory-order architectures like ARM64?
Are independent threads mutating atomic fields that accidentally share the same 64-byte cache line?
Where can `acquire`/`release` semantics replace heavier `seq_cst` full memory fences?

learningJourney.title: Threads, Processes & Coroutines
learningJourney.purpose: Compare OS processes, kernel threads, and M:N user-space green threads under memory and scheduling constraints.
learningJourney.explanation: Concurrency models differ sharply in isolation and scheduling cost. OS processes isolate virtual address spaces (requiring IPC and expensive TLB flushes on switch). Kernel threads (1:1) share memory but reserve 1-8 MB stacks and incur ~1-10 microsecond kernel context switches, limiting concurrency to thousands of threads. M:N schedulers—such as Go's GMP model (Goroutines multiplexed onto OS threads M across logical processors P) and Java Virtual Threads—run user-space tasks with tiny growable stacks (~2 KB) and work-stealing queues, enabling hundreds of thousands of concurrent I/O tasks. However, blocking syscalls or `synchronized` carrier-thread pinning in M:N runtimes can starve peer tasks.

benefits: Preemptive OS scheduling prevents CPU-bound tasks from starving peers.
Direct compatibility with blocking C/OS syscalls and thread-local storage.
costs: 1-8 MB stack reservation limits active threads to low thousands.
Kernel trap and register/scheduler overhead on every blocking context switch.

benefits: ~2 KB initial stacks support 100k+ concurrent I/O tasks with sub-microsecond user-space switches.
Work-stealing keeps all CPU cores balanced without kernel intervention.
costs: Carrier-thread pinning (e.g., JNI or Java `synchronized` blocks) stalls all multiplexed tasks.
Requires cooperative yield points or runtime preemption for CPU-heavy loops.

ideas.title: Go GMP Work-Stealing
ideas.description: Each logical processor P owns a lock-free local run queue; when idle, P steals half the tasks from a busy peer P to balance load with minimal contention.

ideas.title: Carrier-Thread Pinning Hazard
ideas.description: In Java Virtual Threads, entering a `synchronized` block around blocking I/O pins the OS carrier thread; replace with `ReentrantLock` to allow unmounting.

example.title: Unblocking 40,000 concurrent connections by fixing Virtual Thread pinning
example.scenario: A Java 21 payment gateway migrated from a 500-thread pool to Virtual Threads, yet throughput collapsed under load with 90% idle CPU.
example.reasoning: Flight Recorder (`jdk.VirtualThreadPinned`) revealed that a legacy connection pool used `synchronized` around socket reads, pinning all 16 OS carrier threads. Replacing `synchronized` with `ReentrantLock` allowed virtual threads to unmount during I/O, scaling to 40,000 concurrent connections at 1/5th the heap.
example.lesson: M:N coroutines only scale when blocking I/O never pins the underlying OS carrier threads.

reflectionQuestions: Is your concurrency bottleneck CPU-bound computation (favors 1:1 core-sized threads) or high-fanout I/O wait (favors M:N coroutines)?
Which legacy libraries or locks in your stack can pin carrier threads or block an async event loop?
How much virtual and physical memory is consumed by thread stacks at peak concurrency?
How does Python's GIL or runtime scheduler affect multi-core parallelism for your workload?

learningJourney.title: Locks, Mutexes & Synchronization Primitives
learningJourney.purpose: Understand futex fast/slow paths, spinlocks, read-write starvation, and condition variable invariants.
learningJourney.explanation: Modern mutexes optimize for the common uncontended case using a two-tier design: a user-space atomic CAS flips the lock state from 0 to 1 with zero kernel syscalls; only when contended does the thread invoke a Linux `futex(FUTEX_WAIT)` syscall to sleep in a kernel wait queue. Spinlocks avoid sleeping and are viable only for sub-microsecond critical sections when the holder cannot be preempted—otherwise spinning burns 100% CPU while the holder is descheduled. Read-Write locks allow concurrent readers, but naive reader-preferring designs starve writers indefinitely, and high-frequency reader atomic increments still bounce cache lines across cores. Condition variables always require a `while (!predicate)` loop to guard against spurious wakeups.

ideas.title: User-Space Futex Fast Path
ideas.description: Uncontended lock/unlock executes purely via user-space atomic CAS; kernel transitions occur only when threads must park or wake.

ideas.title: SeqLock & RCU for Read-Mostly State
ideas.description: When reads outnumber writes 1000:1, sequence locks or immutable pointer swaps let readers proceed without writing to shared lock cache lines.

example.title: Eliminating RWLock cache-line ping-pong on 64-core feature flags
example.scenario: An ad-routing service checked feature flags under a shared `RWLock` on every request, yet p99 latency degraded from 50 microseconds to 1.2ms as core count scaled to 64.
example.reasoning: Even shared read locks perform an atomic increment/decrement on the lock counter, causing 64 cores to contend on one cache line. Switching to an immutable-snapshot pointer swap (RCU-style atomic load) eliminated reader writes and cut p99 read latency to 180 nanoseconds.
example.lesson: At high core counts, shared read-write locks still contend on the reader reference-count cache line.

reflectionQuestions: How long is the critical section held—nanoseconds (adaptive/spin) or milliseconds (mutex/sharded lock)?
Can you shrink the critical section by computing values before acquiring the lock and performing I/O after releasing it?
Does your Read-Write lock prevent writer starvation under continuous read traffic?
Are all `condvar.wait()` calls wrapped in a `while` loop checking the state predicate?

learningJourney.title: Lock-Free & Wait-Free Data Structures
learningJourney.purpose: Build CAS-based lock-free progress while defeating the ABA problem and unsafe memory reclamation.
learningJourney.explanation: Blocking locks risk priority inversion and convoying when a lock holder is preempted. Lock-free algorithms guarantee system-wide progress (at least one thread finishes in finite steps) using atomic Read-Modify-Write primitives like Compare-And-Swap (CAS) and Fetch-And-Add (FAA); wait-free algorithms guarantee every thread finishes in bounded steps. However, CAS loops suffer two subtle hazards: the ABA problem, where Thread 1 reads value A, gets preempted while Thread 2 changes A -> B -> A (freeing and reallocating the same address), and Thread 1's CAS succeeds on a stale logical state; and memory reclamation, where freeing a removed node while a concurrent reader still holds its pointer causes use-after-free. Tagged pointers (pointer + monotonic version counter via double-width CAS) solve ABA, while Hazard Pointers or Epoch-Based Reclamation (EBR) defer `free()` safely.

ideas.title: Double-Width Tagged Pointers
ideas.description: Pair each pointer with a monotonic 64-bit version tag (`CMPXCHG16B`) so recycled addresses never match stale CAS expectations.

ideas.title: Epoch-Based Reclamation (EBR)
ideas.description: Threads enter a read-side epoch before dereferencing lock-free nodes; retired nodes are freed only after all active threads advance past that epoch.

example.title: Solving ABA use-after-free in a lock-free MPMC job queue
example.scenario: A C++ lock-free stack/queue backed by a custom node free-list crashed intermittently under heavy multi-core churn with corrupted next pointers.
example.reasoning: A preempted consumer held a pointer to node A while another thread popped A, pushed B, and pushed recycled A back to the head—passing the naive pointer CAS. Adding a 64-bit monotonic version tag (`CMPXCHG16B`) and epoch-based reclamation eliminated all crashes at 8M ops/sec.
example.lesson: A lock-free CAS structure without ABA versioning and safe memory reclamation (EBR or Hazard Pointers) is memory-unsafe.

reflectionQuestions: Have you measured lock contention first, or are you introducing lock-free complexity where a simple sharded mutex has zero contention?
How does your CAS structure prevent ABA pointer reuse across node recycling?
Which memory reclamation scheme (GC, Hazard Pointers, or EBR) guarantees readers never dereference freed nodes?
Under extreme contention, does your CAS loop use exponential backoff to avoid saturating the cache-coherence interconnect?

learningJourney.title: Concurrency Bugs: Deadlocks, Livelocks & Starvation
learningJourney.purpose: Prevent and detect deadlocks, livelocks, and priority inversion across threads and databases.
learningJourney.explanation: Deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions simultaneously: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. Breaking Circular Wait is the cleanest structural defense: enforce a strict global lock ordering (e.g., always lock the lower account ID before the higher ID) so cycles are mathematically impossible. Where dynamic ordering is unavoidable (like database row locks), engines maintain Wait-For Graphs (WFG) and run cycle detection to abort the younger transaction, or use bounded `tryLock` timeouts. Note that naive `tryLock` + immediate retry causes livelock—threads burn 100% CPU yielding to each other unless randomized exponential backoff is added. Priority inversion occurs when a low-priority thread holds a lock needed by a high-priority thread while medium-priority threads preempt it, solved by Priority Inheritance.

ideas.title: Deterministic Lock Ordering
ideas.description: Sort multi-resource locks by a canonical key (e.g. `min(idA, idB)` before `max(idA, idB)`) to break Circular Wait structurally.

ideas.title: Avoid Blocking Inside Event Loops
ideas.description: Calling synchronous `.get()` or `.join()` on an async future from inside a fixed event-loop pool causes instant thread-starvation deadlock.

example.title: Eliminating ledger transfer deadlocks via canonical account ordering
example.scenario: Concurrent `transfer(A -> B)` and `transfer(B -> A)` database transactions deadlocked repeatedly under load, forcing 8% transaction aborts.
example.reasoning: Enforced deterministic row-lock ordering (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` ordered by `account_id ASC`) so every multi-account transfer acquires locks in the exact same global direction. Circular wait became impossible, cutting deadlock aborts to zero.
example.lesson: Global lock ordering eliminates circular-wait deadlocks at zero runtime coordination cost.

reflectionQuestions: Which code paths acquire more than one lock simultaneously, and are they ordered by a strict global key?
If you rely on `tryLock` timeouts, do retries use randomized backoff + jitter to prevent livelock?
Could a callback or blocking `.get()` run on the same thread pool as the task it is waiting for (pool-induced deadlock)?
How does your database or runtime detect and break Wait-For Graph cycles?

learningJourney.title: Thread Pools, Work-Stealing & Task Queues
learningJourney.purpose: Size worker pools with Little's Law, bound task queues, and apply work-stealing deques.
learningJourney.explanation: Thread pools decouple task submission from execution, but misconfigured pools cause OOMs or thrashing. By Little's Law (L = lambda * W), optimal concurrency depends on workload type: CPU-bound pools should stay near N_cores to avoid context-switch overhead, whereas blocking I/O pools scale as N_cores * (1 + WaitTime / ServiceTime). Unbounded queues (like Java's default `LinkedBlockingQueue`) hide slow consumers until the heap explodes with `OutOfMemoryError`. Always use bounded queues paired with explicit rejection policies: `AbortPolicy` (fail fast with 429/503), `CallerRunsPolicy` (apply natural backpressure by making the submitter execute the task), or `DiscardOldestPolicy` (for real-time telemetry). For recursive fork-join workloads, Chase-Lev work-stealing deques let owners push/pop LIFO for cache warmth while idle thieves steal FIFO from the opposite end.

ideas.title: Isolate CPU vs. I/O Pools
ideas.description: Never run slow blocking I/O on a core-sized CPU pool or heavy compute on an event-loop pool; give each workload class a dedicated bounded bulkhead.

ideas.title: Bounded Queues + CallerRuns
ideas.description: Cap queue depth to bound tail latency (QueueTime = Depth / Throughput) and use CallerRuns or explicit load shedding when saturated.

example.title: Preventing OOM crashes in an image-processing worker
example.scenario: A thumbnail service using `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16)` (unbounded queue) suffered silent latency climbs followed by `OutOfMemoryError` crashes whenever upstream uploads spiked.
example.reasoning: Replaced the unbounded queue with an `ArrayBlockingQueue(512)` and `CallerRunsPolicy`, and isolated health checks onto a separate management pool. Queue depth stayed bounded, upstream callers felt immediate backpressure, and OOM crashes stopped completely.
example.lesson: An unbounded task queue is a delayed OutOfMemoryError; bound every queue and define its rejection policy.

reflectionQuestions: What is the maximum queue wait time (QueueCapacity / ServiceRate) before queued requests breach your SLA?
Are CPU-bound tasks and blocking I/O tasks isolated in separate thread pools?
Which rejection policy (Abort, CallerRuns, or DiscardOldest) matches your caller contract when the bounded queue fills?
Does your fork-join workload risk deadlocking if child tasks are submitted to the same bounded pool as blocked parent tasks?

learningJourney.title: Reactive Streams, Event Loops & Backpressure
learningJourney.purpose: Scale high-concurrency I/O with non-blocking epoll/Reactor loops and demand-driven backpressure.
learningJourney.explanation: Solving the C10K+ connection problem requires decoupling connections from OS threads. Legacy `select` and `poll` scan O(N) file descriptors on every syscall; Linux `epoll` (and BSD `kqueue`) registers sockets in a kernel red-black tree and returns only ready descriptors in O(1) per ready event, while `io_uring` eliminates syscall overhead via shared submission/completion ring buffers. Event-loop frameworks (Netty, Redis, Node.js) run a Reactor loop that dispatches ready I/O callbacks without blocking—meaning even a single 50ms blocking database call freezes all connections on that loop. To prevent fast producers from overwhelming slow consumers, the Reactive Streams specification enforces pull-based backpressure (`subscription.request(n)`), propagating downstream capacity limits all the way back to TCP `SO_RCVBUF` flow control.

ideas.title: Golden Rule of Event Loops
ideas.description: Never block an event-loop thread with synchronous I/O, `Thread.sleep`, or heavy CPU work; offload blocking work to dedicated bounded worker pools.

ideas.title: Demand-Driven `request(n)` Backpressure
ideas.description: Downstream subscribers signal exact capacity `n` upstream so memory stays bounded and TCP zero-window throttling slows fast producers.

example.title: Taming a 100,000-sensor IoT reconnection storm with backpressure
example.scenario: When 100,000 IoT devices reconnected simultaneously after a carrier outage, an ingestion service buffered incoming telemetry in memory until consumer pods crashed with OOMs.
example.reasoning: Adopted Project Reactor with bounded ring buffers and `request(n)` pull backpressure wired to Netty socket auto-read toggling. When downstream storage reached 80% buffer capacity, Netty paused socket reads, letting TCP flow control throttle devices cleanly with zero dropped packets or OOMs.
example.lesson: True backpressure propagates downstream capacity all the way to socket read-pause and TCP flow control.

reflectionQuestions: Could any synchronous driver, DNS lookup, or heavy JSON parse block your Reactor event-loop threads?
How does your streaming pipeline propagate slow-consumer backpressure to the network edge?
What happens to memory if a fast publisher ignores `request(n)`—are you buffering, dropping, or failing?
How many event-loop threads (typically 1x-2x CPU cores) are optimal before cross-loop coordination hurts?

failureScenario.title: The Stale Lock Zombie Writer (GC Pause Disaster)
failureScenario.reasoning: Worker 1 acquires a 30s distributed lease with fencing token 41 to finalize seat A-12, then freezes for 35s in a Stop-The-World GC pause. The lease expires; Worker 2 acquires token 42 and sells seat A-12. Worker 1 wakes up and attempts to overwrite the seat record.

decisionFramework.question: Can shared mutable state be eliminated via partitioning, immutability, or actor ownership?
decisionFramework.reason: Shared-nothing architectures remove lock contention, memory-barrier bugs, and cache-line bouncing at the root.

decisionFramework.question: Does the workload fit 1:1 threads, M:N coroutines, or a single-threaded event loop?
decisionFramework.reason: Match CPU-bound work to core-sized pools, high-fanout I/O to M:N coroutines/Reactor loops, and never block an event loop.

decisionFramework.question: Are happens-before edges and lock hierarchies explicitly enforced?
decisionFramework.reason: Acquire-release atomics guarantee cross-core visibility; global lock ordering prevents circular-wait deadlocks.

decisionFramework.question: Are all queues bounded with explicit backpressure or shedding policies?
decisionFramework.reason: Unbounded queues convert slow downstream dependencies into silent OutOfMemoryError crashes.

decisionFramework.question: How are distributed locks protected against process pauses and clock skew?
decisionFramework.reason: Pair every distributed lease with a monotonic fencing token verified atomically by the authoritative storage layer.

knowledgeCheck.question: Service A acquires a 10-second Redis distributed lock before updating an S3/database record, but experiences a 15-second GC pause before writing. What prevents Service A from corrupting a newer writer's data?

options.text: Increase the Redis lock TTL to 60 seconds so GC pauses never exceed it.
options.feedback: Arbitrary network delays and pauses have no hard upper bound in asynchronous systems; longer TTLs only delay recovery on real crashes.

options.text: Attach a monotonically increasing fencing token to each lock grant and have the storage layer reject writes with older tokens.
options.feedback: Correct. Even if a client wakes up after its lease expired, the storage layer rejects its lower fencing token atomically.

options.text: Have Service A re-check `GET lock_key` in Redis right before writing to storage.
options.feedback: Check-then-act is still vulnerable to a pause or network delay between the Redis check and the storage write.
